item.content:encoded:
In case this gets another edit:

There is now a well-studied mammalian eusocial species; naked mole rats. At least a rephrasing of the sentence about such social structures only occurring in insects is in order. Comparisons and intimations could also be used to extend the creep factor.

Regarding the redaction, I can think of at least one kind of thing that could be worse than what is described, because it would explicitly take away one's last bit of individuality.

+ show block
– hide block


For example, voluntary and extensive surgery to restructure the reproductive systems of women who were judged reproductively sound, so that their eggs can be placed into "queens" who are malfunctioning in a useful way- they build babies very quickly, but at the sacrifice of their ability to do anything else, just baby-sacks that pump out that horrendously fast population growth. The babies are then given to more normal women whose merit was found to be in mothering, and were therefore turned into permanent wet nurses. The removal of the two sections of reproduction that would otherwise be required of those reproductively worthy women allowing them to serve their other functions more effectively, without failing to pass on those genes.

Due to the way males produce their gametes, you couldn't do quite the same thing, so it's either repeatedly directly inseminating the baby sacks or donating semen for artificial insemination. Which one a particular man is assigned would no doubt again be based on how valuable his time is to the society, with the well-built brain surgeons being encouraged to have a quick wank into a bottle at every opportunity while the brawny but interchangeable laborer has to go down and do his duty in person periodically.

Anyone falling outside useful categories would, of course, be fed immediately to the queens and wet nurses, so there could also be a voluntary and extensive assessment to see which category you fall into, with "immediately useful nutrients" being one possible outcome.

Pretty sure if the assessment is too close to the way the Foundation decides who's worth saving during a breach, that would justify the redaction in-world, too, but you could still reveal it with an 05-level deobfuscation if desired.

item.content:encoded:
I have to disagree with all of the complaints about bad expungement. I think it's great expungement. Better than Procedure 110-Montauk.

This isn't "LeBron James driving an escalade into a Baskin Robins" territory. We get plenty of context and buildup for what might be going on behind that [DATA EXPUNGED]:
- It definitely involves reproduction and pregnancy
- It supports rapid population growth
- It definitely horrified pretty much everyone except the Bond-villain-level-nut-job Alphas, and even they felt they had to hide it.
- The Foundation isn't comfortable talking about it in an article where they openly discuss cannibalism and eugenic suicide (so unless the O5's are major prudes one would assume it's not just a sex thing)
- It happens before conception
- It's voluntary and extensive

No matter how hard I try I can't think of one single thing that fits those criteria, let alone would be more satisfying than not knowing. (I mean seriously, try to plug something in. You got anything?) It's either paragraphs of info gone or something so bizarre that it's clearly beyond me. I'm just spinning my wheels in the best possible way. That's good mystery.

Anyhow, +1 way back. This is one of my favorite SCPs of all time.

item.title: Re: Idea Stolen
item.content:encoded:
but I wish they'd give credit to the SCP Foundation for these awesome ideas.

Granted, no one can really claim if certain ideas are inspired another source or if they are independently conceived without knowledge of other sources. Is there even a need to insist that Person X did Concept Y first and anyone who does it afterwards must have derived from X's portrayal of Y?

In the totality of media and storytelling, there is only a finite set of stories that are expressed via a maybe infinite set of permutations. What matters is the different takes on the same topic, and how even similar stories can be expressed differently to make them stand out.

item.title: Idea Stolen
item.content:encoded:
I know this is not the most unique of ideas, but I feel like Marvel stole this idea in the Ultimate line with Reed Richards' secret underground time-warped society. I love the idea of this SCP, and while the concept might not be absolutely unheard-of, it's still really well-written. Just as I feel 173 was grabbed by Doctor Who to become the Weeping Angels, I think this one was adapted as well.

It's not a bad thing, but I wish they'd give credit to the SCP Foundation for these awesome ideas. There are awesome writers on this site that deserve some recognition for truly creepy ideas that were popularized later.

item.content:encoded: I quite like this. I didn't have any trouble with the population growth because I figured that if these scientists were able to essentially engineer a new species of humans, those humans might not necessarily have the same gestation period and reproductive constraints as Homo sapiens. The inbreeding is a problem to me only if the "litters" are small. If this species is capable of birthing many more offspring at a time, obviously the population can grow more with less copulation. And as stated in the article, they're not morally bound by our morals, so we might see a child of A1 and A2 mating with A3 from the original seed population rather than, say, B2 of their own generation. And they probably start reproducing at a younger age, too, allowing the third generation to go back and mate with an unrelated member of the first generation. Also, the disabled/feeble are clearly whittled out of the population, so individuals manifesting negative qualities wouldn't propagate… That's how my mind sort of circumvented the breeding issues.

It could be argued that "wrong" is relative. From the "survival of the fittest" perspective, it's not wrong at all. Many species behave just as the population of 752 does, as it's the most efficient means of ensuring that successful traits are passed on and unsuccessful ones are not. Our current society definitely does not do this. Humanity is accumulating traits that would be lethal in a natural environment. Those traits that would lead to early death before being able to reproduce in a natural population are being preserved and passed on in modern human society.

But, by our own society's standards, yes, you're wrong. But who's to say which society's standards are right?
